content: To be effective, interventions must be supported by robust research, including both basic and operational studies. The Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhea (GAPPD) is dedicated to advancing research, particularly community-based action research and sociocultural studies that explore knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, cultural practices, and health-seeking behaviors. As countries scale up interventions, research will also be needed to refine delivery strategies, address barriers to implementation, and identify improved methods for execution. However, the need for research should not delay the immediate implementation of proven interventions. Efforts to control pneumonia and diarrhea in children must also focus on building research capacity in the countries most affected by these diseases. The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) have generated significant momentum and strengthened political commitment to child survival and development. Since 1990, substantial reductions in under-five mortality have saved millions of young lives, largely due to the adoption of basic health interventions alongside improvements in economic conditions, female education, and technology. However, as the 2015 MDG deadline approached, much work remained to be done, extending through at least 2025. The GAPPD provides a framework to accelerate progress in preventing and controlling the leading causes of child mortality during the countdown to 2015 and beyond. This opportunity to advocate for and secure increased investment in pneumonia and diarrhea should not be overlooked. Given the global burden of these diseases, the resources required to implement proven interventions are relatively modest. Additionally, there is widespread recognition that reducing global health problems requires active community involvement, supported by effective international partnerships and collaborative efforts. Policies and actions are already laying the foundation for this community-based approach. Despite progress, the global MDG 4 target of reducing child mortality by two-thirds remains out of reach for many of the world's poorest countries. Approximately 5 billion people still lack access to improved sanitation. Achieving health targets for children beyond 2015 will require urgent action on pneumonia and diarrhea from national governments and global partners. Coordinated and integrated action at international, national, and sub-national levels, as outlined in the GAPPD, is urgently needed. In a rapidly changing world, programs addressing diarrhea and pneumonia must remain flexible, capable of assessing risks, and adaptable to evolving contexts. Specific goals include reducing pneumonia mortality in children under five by 65% and the incidence of severe pneumonia by 25% by 2015, compared to 2000 levels. Targets include achieving 90% coverage of relevant vaccines, 90% access to appropriate pneumonia case management, and 90% exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. Key strategies for addressing pneumonia include case management at all levels, vaccination, prevention and management of HIV infection, improved nutrition, reduction of low birth weight, and control of indoor air pollution. Five interventions could significantly reduce pneumonia mortality and morbidity: effective case management, achieving immunization targets, promoting exclusive breastfeeding and zinc supplementation, reducing indoor air pollution, and improving HIV prevention and management. Similarly, a comprehensive seven-point action plan for diarrhea control emphasizes treatment through fluid replacement to prevent dehydration and zinc supplementation. Oral rehydration therapy (ORT), particularly with low-osmolarity ORS, remains the cornerstone of treatment, alongside continued feeding and breastfeeding during diarrhea episodes. Prevention strategies include improving water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) practices, promoting rotavirus vaccination, and integrating behavior change communication to enhance community uptake of interventions. Achieving universal access to safe drinking water, hygienic sanitation, and handwashing facilities is critical for reducing diarrheal disease incidence and achieving broader health and development goals. Regular training, supervision, and motivation of health workers are essential. Community health workers (CHWs) can play a vital role in diagnosing and treating childhood pneumonia and diarrhea, particularly in areas with limited access to health facilities. Efforts should build on existing strategies, target high-risk areas, and integrate with other relevant programs, such as those addressing malaria, nutrition, and integrated management of childhood illnesses (IMCI).
